analysis.one_liner: Bans broadband providers from blocking, slowing, or charging websites extra fees to reach customers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from March 2006 until the Congress ended in January 2007, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every company that owns or controls an Internet connection to treat all websites, applications, and services equally. Providers could not slow down or block competing content, favor their own services, or charge online companies a fee to deliver traffic to subscribers. Companies could still block spam, viruses, and other harmful traffic, and anyone harmed by a violation could complain to the Federal Communications Commission, which would have 90 days to rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users, who would keep equal access to every website without their provider slowing or surcharging sites; and online businesses, from large content companies to small sellers and startups, which would reach customers without paying broadband providers a toll for the same speed everyone else gets.

how_it_helps.text: Network operators could not block, degrade, or alter any content, application, or service transmitted over their networks, and could not discriminate in allocating bandwidth, including in favor of themselves or affiliated companies.
Providers could not charge fees to outside application or service providers for delivering traffic to subscribers, closing off a paid-prioritization revenue model before it started.

Consumers would get access to unaffiliated content and services on the same terms as the provider's own offerings, without interference or surcharges, and providers would have to post all rates, terms, and conditions for public inspection.

A hurt party could file a complaint with the FCC; the agency would have 7 days to accept the case and 90 days to issue a final decision, with the burden of proof on the network operator and a cease-and-desist requirement in the meantime.

The bill preserved operators' authority to block spam, viruses, adware, spyware, pornography, and content inappropriate for minors, as long as subscribers were informed and could disable the blocking.

analysis.who_pays: Cable and telephone broadband providers, which would lose the ability to favor their own services, sell faster delivery to preferred websites, or condition access to their subscribers on payment from online companies.

drawbacks.text: Strict nondiscrimination and 90-day deemed-violation rules could constrain operators' ability to manage congestion and could impose real compliance costs, though the bill expressly preserved reasonable security and anti-spam measures with subscriber opt-out.

Broadband providers argued, in the wider debate over net neutrality, that being barred from charging content companies for priority delivery would reduce their incentive and revenue for network investment; the bill's findings instead leaned on the fact that most Americans had little or no choice of high-speed provider.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered strong, enforceable protection for the open Internet at a time when the bill's own findings showed only about 2 percent of Americans had a broadband choice beyond the local phone or cable company, so consumer bargaining power was thin. The costs fell almost entirely on broadband providers' ability to build a paid-prioritization business, and the main open question was whether that constraint would slow network investment. On the consumer side, the design was unusually detailed: fast complaint deadlines, operator burden of proof, and automatic violation findings if the FCC missed its deadline.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced it in March 2006, the Senate sent it to the Commerce Committee, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the Internet Non-Discrimination Act of 2006 on March 2, 2006.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the only later entry in the action history is Wyden's introductory remarks in June 2006.
The bill ended the 109th Congress with zero cosponsors, having never advanced beyond referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband and cable providers, which kept full freedom to manage, prioritize, and charge for network access as they saw fit; the open-Internet rules Wyden proposed did not take effect.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it twice, in March and June 2006.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ted Stevens (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral; no hearing, markup, or report on the bill through the end of the Congress.

against.name: Cable and telephone broadband industry
against.role: Network operators targeted by the bill's nondiscrimination and anti-charging rules
against.what_they_did: Opposed government net-neutrality mandates during the 2006 debate, arguing providers should manage their networks and price paid priority as they saw fit.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the only sponsor was a Democrat and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from blocking or degrading content, favoring their own services, and charging outside websites for delivering traffic to their subscribers, ending a paid-prioritization revenue model before it formed. Consumers' interest in an open Internet ran directly against these revenue options.

industries.industry: Online content, application, and service providers
industries.note: Websites and app makers from major platforms to small sellers would reach users without paying broadband tolls or facing throttling in favor of the provider's own offerings. This is the same interest ordinary Internet users have in equal access.
